messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 38
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Welder
  trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another
  pcl5: 60

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid People: avoid other people, Avoid Thinking: Thinking about the event, Self-Blame Rumination: I dwell on what I have done wrong
  Threat: Sleep Problems: Trouble falling or staying asleep, Concentration: Having difficulty concentrating, Physical Reactivity: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience
  Memory: Taste Vividness: I can taste what I tasted during the event when the memory returns, Incomplete Picture: I feel like I am only remembering parts of what happened and the rest is missing, Guilt on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense guilt

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

# Clinical Vignette: Thuy Nguyen

Thuy Nguyen, thirty-eight, has worked as a welder for fifteen years—long enough to know the weight of metal, the geometry of joints, the precise angle at which a torch must meet steel. She learned the trade from her father, who learned it from his father in Hanoi before the family came to California when she was seven. Welding was supposed to be her inheritance, something solid and knowable in a life that had never been either. Until eighteen months ago, it became the thing she could no longer hold.

It happened on a Tuesday morning in March. Thuy was working on a structural repair at a commercial construction site, a routine job she had completed dozens of times. Her colleague, Marcus, was positioned on the opposite side of the beam she was welding, holding a guide rod in place. The work was methodical, practiced. Thuy's hands moved with the sureness of someone who had done this ten thousand times. But the rod Marcus was holding—she had come to believe, in the endless replaying, that she had not checked it properly before he took position. When she struck the arc, something shifted. The heat was tremendous, sudden. Marcus screamed. The rod had not been secured correctly, and the contact point burned directly into his forearm. Thuy killed the torch immediately, but the damage was already done. She remembered the smell—not the usual metal-and-flux smell of welding, but something else, something organic and charred. She could still taste it: a metallic bitterness at the back of her throat, like blood mixed with copper, that would return without warning. The taste alone could transport her back to that moment, her hands frozen, Marcus's face contorted.

Marcus spent three weeks in the hospital. He recovered, eventually, though his arm bears permanent scarring and he transferred to a different job site. He never blamed Thuy directly. The investigation concluded the accident resulted from a positioning error, but did not assign fault. None of that mattered to Thuy. She had come to believe with absolute certainty that she had been careless, that her failure to double-check the setup had caused another person's suffering. This conviction lived in her body. When she tried to sleep at night, her mind would loop through the moment—but only fragments of it. She could recall the sound of the torch igniting, Marcus's scream, the smell, the taste. But the moments before felt clouded, incomplete. What exactly had she been thinking? Had she been distracted? She could not quite access the full sequence, and the gaps made her certain she was forgetting something crucial, something that would prove her negligence beyond doubt.

Within weeks, Thuy began avoiding the workshop. She called in sick, and then requested a temporary reassignment to administrative tasks. She told her supervisor she needed time to process the accident. What she did not say was that she could not bear to be around the equipment, could not stand the thought of seeing Marcus's empty station, could not trust her own hands anymore. At night, when her mind would turn toward the event—and it always did—she would lie awake for hours, her heart racing, her body rigid. When sleep finally came, it was shallow and broken. She began avoiding her coworkers entirely, eating lunch alone in her truck instead of joining the crew, declining after-work gatherings. She was certain they blamed her, even if they said they didn't. She couldn't bear to see it in their faces.

The rumination became her constant companion. She would sit at home and replay what she had done wrong, constructing scenarios in which she had checked the rod, in which she had caught the error, in which Marcus was not scarred. When she tried to focus on anything else—reading, watching television, conversations—her mind would fracture. She could not hold a thought that was not about the accident. At work, when she attempted to return to welding tasks, her hands would shake uncontrollably. Her heart would pound. Sometimes she felt dizzy, as though the ground was tilting. Once, a coworker's radio played a song that had been on the day of the accident, and Thuy had to leave the site.

She has not welded in six months. Her supervisor has been patient, but the reassignments cannot continue indefinitely. Thuy knows this. She also knows that she cannot go back to the work that defined her, not as long as she remains convinced that her carelessness, her fundamental failure of attention, makes her a danger to anyone near her. It was her daughter, home from college for a weekend, who finally insisted she see someone. Thuy had been distant with her, unable to explain why she flinched at loud noises or why she seemed so hollowed out. "Mom," her daughter had said, "you need help." Thuy had agreed, not because she believed help was possible, but because she had run out of ways to live with what she had done.
